standing_assumptions: The work is a three-page note (Statistics and Probability Letters 106 (2015) 100–102) with one proposition and one corollary. Everything below was read from the rendered page images. [Estimator: Section 1, p. 100 (PDF p. 1)] “Many researchers have approximated RDS as a sampling design in which the sampling probability for subject $i$ is proportional to their network degree $d_i$ (Salganik and Heckathorn, 2004; Volz and Heckathorn, 2008; Gile and Handcock, 2010; Gile, 2011). In particular, Salganik and Heckathorn (2004) and Volz and Heckathorn (2008) justify this choice by modeling the recruitment process as a with-replacement random walk on a connected population network, where only one coupon is given to each subject, recruitment is uniformly at random from network neighbors, and each subject can be recruited infinitely many times. For an RDS sample of size $n$, Volz and Heckathorn (2008) (hereafter VH) give the estimator $$\hat{\mu}_{VH} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i d_i^{-1}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i^{-1}} \qquad (1)$$ where $y_i$ is the outcome of interest and $d_i$ is the degree of subject $i$.” [Setting: Section 2, first paragraph, p. 101 (PDF p. 2)] “Formally, consider a sequence of populations and samples converging weakly to a joint limit distribution on the outcome, (reported) degree, and sample, denoted $(Y, D, S)$. Let the $\mathrm{E}[\cdot]$ and $\Pr[\cdot]$ operators refer to features of this limiting distribution. In RDS, we observe the empirical joint distribution of the outcome $Y$ and degree $D$ conditional on the sampling indicator $S = 1$. Without loss of generality, suppose that $Y$ has bounded support and that $D$ has support in the set $\{1, \ldots, K\}$.” [Condition 1: p. 101 (PDF p. 2)] “Condition 1 (Ignorability). For all $k$ such that $\Pr[D = k] > 0$, $\mathrm{E}[Y|S = 1, D = k] = \mathrm{E}[Y|D = k]$ and $\Pr[S = 1|D = k] > 0$.” [Condition 2: p. 101 (PDF p. 2)] “Condition 2 (Knowledge of the Conditional Probability of Sampling). $\Pr[S = 1|D = k] = cf(k)$, where $f(\cdot)$ is known and $c$ is an unknown scale parameter.” [What the paper does not print] The paper gives no further definition of: the sense in which ‘populations and samples’ converge weakly (which empirical measure converges, and in which mode when the sample is random); whether ‘bounded support’ is a bound on each population in the sequence or on the limiting $Y$ only; the range of $k$ in Condition 2 and in the sums of (2) and (4) (Condition 1 alone carries ‘for all $k$ such that $\Pr[D = k] > 0$’); the signs of $c$ and $f$; the words ‘identified’ and ‘consistent’; and how the indicator $S$ and the index $i = 1, \ldots, n$ of (1) are related when a subject can be recruited more than once. [Remarks for the formalizer, not printed in the paper] The readings the audit's validators settled on are: $(Y, D, S)$ has a fixed probability law $F$ on $\mathbb{R} \times \{1, \ldots, K\} \times \{0, 1\}$ with $Y$ bounded, $K$ a positive integer, and $\mathrm{E}$, $\Pr$ are taken under $F$; Conditions 1 and 2 are conditions on $F$; conditional quantities given $D = k$ are used only for $k \in A = \{k : \Pr[D = k] > 0\}$, and Condition 2 and the sums in (2) and (4) are read over $A$ (finding P021-N003, rated a clarity note); the bounds on outcomes and degrees are standing assumptions common to every population in the sequence, not reductions (finding P021-E001, rated a clarity note); the opening sentence of Section 2 is the standing assumption that the realized joint empirical laws of the populations with their samples converge weakly to $F$, in probability if they are random (candidate P021-N004, not confirmed as an error by either validator). [Why the list has two targets] No finding rated as an error in this work concerns a mathematical statement: the two errors (P021-E002 and P021-N001, both Minor) are bibliographic misprints, P021-E001 and P021-N003 are clarity notes, and P021-N002 and P021-N004 were not confirmed. There is therefore no counterexample, corrected-statement or result-touched-by-finding target; what the validators established under the two clarity notes is recorded in the notes of the two targets, because a formal statement needs it. Of the six headline claims, H1 (Proposition 1) and H2 (Corollary 1) are mathematical statements. H3 to H6 (the comparison with the random-walk model, the remark that ignorability given degree alone does not identify the mean, the remark that the two conditions have no directly testable implications, and the remark on diagnostics) are Discussion remarks that both fresh readers classed as interpretive or as a recommendation, and they are not targets.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 1, with Eq. (2) and the printed proof, Eqs. (3)–(4)
canonical_claim.statement: [Setting, Section 2, first paragraph, p. 101 (PDF p. 2)] Formally, consider a sequence of populations and samples converging weakly to a joint limit distribution on the outcome, (reported) degree, and sample, denoted $(Y, D, S)$. Let the $\mathrm{E}[\cdot]$ and $\Pr[\cdot]$ operators refer to features of this limiting distribution. In RDS, we observe the empirical joint distribution of the outcome $Y$ and degree $D$ conditional on the sampling indicator $S = 1$. Without loss of generality, suppose that $Y$ has bounded support and that $D$ has support in the set $\{1, \ldots, K\}$. [p. 101] Condition 1 (Ignorability). For all $k$ such that $\Pr[D = k] > 0$, $\mathrm{E}[Y|S = 1, D = k] = \mathrm{E}[Y|D = k]$ and $\Pr[S = 1|D = k] > 0$. [p. 101] Condition 2 (Knowledge of the Conditional Probability of Sampling). $\Pr[S = 1|D = k] = cf(k)$, where $f(\cdot)$ is known and $c$ is an unknown scale parameter. [p. 101] Proposition 1. Given Conditions 1 and 2, the population mean is identified, with $$\mathrm{E}[Y] = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathrm{E}[Y|S = 1, D = k]\,\frac{\Pr[D=k|S=1]}{f(k)}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{\Pr[D=k|S=1]}{f(k)}}. \qquad (2)$$ [Proof as printed, p. 101] Proof. We can identify $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = k]$ for each degree $k$ from Condition 1 since $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = k] = \mathrm{E}[Y|S = 1, D = k]$. We can identify each $\Pr[D = k]$ to scale directly from Condition 2 as $$\Pr[D = k] = \frac{\Pr[D = k|S = 1]\,\Pr[S = 1]}{\Pr[S = 1|D = k]} = \frac{\Pr[S = 1]}{c}\,\frac{\Pr[D = k|S = 1]}{f(k)}. \qquad (3)$$ Then by the law of total expectation, $$\mathrm{E}[Y] = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathrm{E}[Y|D = k]\,\frac{\Pr[S=1]}{c}\,\frac{\Pr[D=k|S=1]}{f(k)}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{\Pr[S=1]}{c}\,\frac{\Pr[D=k|S=1]}{f(k)}} = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathrm{E}[Y|D = k]\,\frac{\Pr[D=k|S=1]}{f(k)}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{\Pr[D=k|S=1]}{f(k)}}. \qquad (4)$$ $\square$ [The hypotheses printed are the setting and Conditions 1 and 2 above. No range of $k$ is printed in Condition 2, and the sums in (2) and (4) are printed from $k = 1$ to $K$.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [$(Y, D, S)$, $\mathrm{E}[\cdot]$, $\Pr[\cdot]$: Section 2, first paragraph, p. 101 (PDF p. 2)] the outcome, the (reported) degree and the sample (the ‘sampling indicator’, with $S = 1$ for sampled units) under the joint limit distribution; the operators refer to that distribution. $Y$ has bounded support and $D$ has support in $\{1, \ldots, K\}$ (same paragraph). [Conditions 1 and 2: p. 101] as transcribed in the statement. [$f$, $c$: Condition 2, p. 101] $f(\cdot)$ a known function of degree and $c$ an unknown scale parameter; no sign or range is printed. [Conditional quantities] $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = k]$, $\mathrm{E}[Y|S = 1, D = k]$, $\Pr[S = 1|D = k]$ and $\Pr[D = k|S = 1]$ are not defined beyond the notation; they are the elementary conditional expectations and probabilities, defined when the conditioning event has positive probability. [What is observed: p. 101] ‘In RDS, we observe the empirical joint distribution of the outcome $Y$ and degree $D$ conditional on the sampling indicator $S = 1$’; so the observable is the law of $(Y, D)$ given $S = 1$, and $\Pr[S = 1]$ and $c$ are not observed. [Identified] Not defined in the paper. Read by both fresh readers and the validator as: $\mathrm{E}[Y]$ equals an expression in the law of $(Y, D)$ given $S = 1$ and the known $f$ only, which is what the right side of (2) is. [$K$] Not defined beyond the phrase quoted; a positive integer.

The right side of (v) is also unchanged when $f$ is replaced by $\lambda f$ with $\lambda

Index range (finding P021-N003; it is rated a clarity note, so there is no corrected-statement target, but a formal statement has to settle the point). Condition 2, the proof's ‘for each degree $k$’ and the sums $\sum_{k=1}^{K}$ in (2) and (4) are printed without the restriction to $\Pr[D = k] > 0$ that Condition 1 carries, and the setting says only that $D$ ‘has support in’ $\{1, \ldots, K\}$. The validator confirmed that, read literally at a $k$ with $\Pr[D = k] = 0$, the $k$th term involves conditional quantities on a null event and can be $0/0$: with $K = 3$, $p = (1/2, 0, 1/2)$, $f = (1, 0, 3)$, $c = 1/4$, $Y = 0$ at $D = 1$ and $Y = 1$ at $D = 3$, one has $ho = 1/2$ and $q = (1/4, 0, 3/4)$, the $k = 2$ weight is $0/0$, and the sums over $A = \{1, 3\}$ give $(1/4)/(1/2) = 1/2 = \mathrm{E}[Y]$. With the sums over $A$ the proposition and its proof are correct and no assumption is added; when $A = \{1, \ldots, K\}$ the printed display and (v) are the same. A formal statement should sum over $A$, or say which convention it uses for the terms with $q_k = 0$ (if those terms are taken to be zero, the printed sums equal the sums over $A$), so that it can be compared with the printed display. Separate signs $c > 0$ and $f > 0$ are not needed: only $c f(k) > 0$ on $A$, which Condition 1 gives. Other points. Condition 1 is mean ignorability within degree classes: $S$ may depend on $Y$ within a class provided the two conditional means agree, and conditional independence of $Y$ and $S$ given $D$ must not be assumed. The proposition is an exact identity for the single law $F$ (in the paper, the limiting distribution); no convergence enters, and boundedness of $Y$ serves only to make the expectations finite (integrability is enough). The words ‘Without loss of generality’ in the setting are the subject of finding P021-E001 (a clarity note): bounded $Y$ and $D \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ are assumptions of the statement, not reductions. Worked instance, recomputed in exact arithmetic when this list was fixed: $p = (1/2, 1/3, 1/6)$, $f(k) = k$, $c = 1/4$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = k] = (0, 1, 2)$ give $ho = 5/12$, $q = (3/10, 2/5, 3/10)$, numerator $2/5$, denominator $3/5$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y] = 2/3$; the $K = 3$ example above was recomputed as well. Both fresh readers report that the claim held up (one with the index-range caveat). The validator's derivation is the section ‘N003: support convention and exact derivation’ of the artifact named here; its exact example is runs/P021/validate/_batch/P021-B01/work/check_support.py, with output check_support-output.json in the same folder.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Corollary 1, with the sentence introducing it and the VH estimator, Eq. (1)
canonical_claim.location: p. 101 (PDF p. 2); Eq. (1) is on p. 100 (PDF p. 1)
canonical_claim.statement: [Sentence introducing the corollary, p. 101 (PDF p. 2)] Given Proposition 1, consistency of the VH estimator directly follows from convergence of sample analogues to population quantities. [p. 101] Corollary 1. Given Conditions 1 and 2, the VH estimator is consistent for $\mathrm{E}[Y]$ if $f(k) \propto k$. [The VH estimator, p. 100 (PDF p. 1)] For an RDS sample of size $n$, Volz and Heckathorn (2008) (hereafter VH) give the estimator $$\hat{\mu}_{VH} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i d_i^{-1}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i^{-1}} \qquad (1)$$ where $y_i$ is the outcome of interest and $d_i$ is the degree of subject $i$. [Setting, Section 2, first paragraph, p. 101] Formally, consider a sequence of populations and samples converging weakly to a joint limit distribution on the outcome, (reported) degree, and sample, denoted $(Y, D, S)$. Let the $\mathrm{E}[\cdot]$ and $\Pr[\cdot]$ operators refer to features of this limiting distribution. In RDS, we observe the empirical joint distribution of the outcome $Y$ and degree $D$ conditional on the sampling indicator $S = 1$. Without loss of generality, suppose that $Y$ has bounded support and that $D$ has support in the set $\{1, \ldots, K\}$. [p. 101] Condition 1 (Ignorability). For all $k$ such that $\Pr[D = k] > 0$, $\mathrm{E}[Y|S = 1, D = k] = \mathrm{E}[Y|D = k]$ and $\Pr[S = 1|D = k] > 0$. [p. 101] Condition 2 (Knowledge of the Conditional Probability of Sampling). $\Pr[S = 1|D = k] = cf(k)$, where $f(\cdot)$ is known and $c$ is an unknown scale parameter. [No proof is printed beyond the sentence introducing the corollary. The hypotheses printed are the setting, Conditions 1 and 2 and $f(k) \propto k$. The paper prints no mode of convergence, no definition of ‘consistent’, and no statement of which empirical distribution converges.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [VH estimator: Eq. (1), p. 100 (PDF p. 1)] as transcribed in the statement; $n$ is the size of the RDS sample, $y_i$ the outcome of interest and $d_i$ the degree of subject $i$. [$(Y, D, S)$, $\mathrm{E}[\cdot]$, $\Pr[\cdot]$, bounded support of $Y$, $D \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$: Section 2, first paragraph, p. 101 (PDF p. 2)] as in P021-T1. [Conditions 1 and 2: p. 101] as transcribed. [Proposition 1 and Eq. (2): p. 101] P021-T1. [$f(k) \propto k$] Not defined further; read as $f(k) = ak$ for a constant $a \ne 0$. [Sequence of populations and samples converging weakly to a joint limit distribution] Not defined further in the paper. Read by the validators (P021-E001; both validators of P021-N004) as follows: the $r$th population has $N_r$ units with outcomes $y_{rj}$, degrees $d_{rj}$ and sample membership $s_{rj} \in \{0, 1\}$; its joint empirical law is $F_r = \frac{1}{N_r}\sum_{j=1}^{N_r}\delta_{(y_{rj}, d_{rj}, s_{rj})}$; and $F_r$ converges weakly to the fixed law $F$ of $(Y, D, S)$, in probability when the $F_r$ are random (for every bounded continuous $g$, $\int g\,dF_r \to \int g\,dF$ in probability). [Sample; Eq. (1) on the $r$th sample] The sample is the set of units with $s_{rj} = 1$, of size $n_r = \sum_j s_{rj}$, and $\hat\mu_{VH,r} = \sum_{j : s_{rj} = 1} y_{rj} d_{rj}^{-1} \big/ \sum_{j : s_{rj} = 1} d_{rj}^{-1}$. [Consistent] Not defined in the paper; read as $\hat\mu_{VH,r} \to \mathrm{E}_F[Y]$ in probability (ordinary convergence when populations and samples are deterministic). [Bounded support] Read as a bound common to every population in the sequence: constants $B < \infty$ and $K < \infty$ with $|y_{rj}| \le B$ and $d_{rj} \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ for all $r$ and $j$ (finding P021-E001). [Sample analogues, population quantities] Not defined; in the validators' derivation the sample analogues are the two sample averages of $y_i/d_i$ and $1/d_i$ whose ratio is (1), and the population quantities are $\mathrm{E}[Y/D|S = 1]$ and $\mathrm{E}[1/D|S = 1]$ under $F$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: All exact. None is displayed in the paper apart from Proposition 1 and Eq. (1); they are derived in runs/P021/validate/P021-N004/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 1–4, and in section 4 of the artifact named below. Notation: $F$ the limit law, $A = \{k : \Pr[D = k] > 0\}$, $p_k = \Pr[D = k]$, $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y]$, all under $F$; for the $r$th population, $A_r = \int \frac{sy}{d}\,dF_r = \frac{1}{N_r}\sum_j \frac{s_{rj}y_{rj}}{d_{rj}}$ and $B_r = \int \frac{s}{d}\,dF_r = \frac{1}{N_r}\sum_j \frac{s_{rj}}{d_{rj}}$. (a) [Proposition 1, p. 101 (PDF p. 2)] Eq. (2) with the sums over $A$ (P021-T1). (b) [The limit law at $f(k) = ak$] With $b = ca$: $\Pr[S = 1|D = k] = bk$ for every $k \in A$, and $b > 0$ because $A$ is not empty and Condition 1 gives $bk > 0$ there. Then $\mathrm{E}[S/D] = \sum_{k \in A} p_k\,\frac{bk}{k} = b$ and, using Condition 1, $\mathrm{E}[SY/D] = \sum_{k \in A} p_k\,\frac{bk}{k}\,\mathrm{E}[Y|S = 1, D = k] = b\mu$. Hence $\mathrm{E}[SY/D]/\mathrm{E}[S/D] = \mu$; dividing both by $\Pr[S = 1] > 0$, $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y/D|S = 1]/\mathrm{E}[1/D|S = 1]$, which is Eq. (2) at $f(k) = ak$. (c) [Plug-in identity for each finite population; Eq. (1), p. 100 (PDF p. 1)] If $n_r \ge 1$ then $B_r > 0$ and $\hat\mu_{VH,r} = A_r/B_r$: both sums in (1) run over the units with $s_{rj} = 1$ and the common factor $1/N_r$ cancels. Also $n_r/N_r = \int s\,dF_r$. (d) [Test functions] On $[-B, B] \times \{1, \ldots, K\} \times \{0, 1\}$ the functions $(y, d, s) \mapsto sy/d$, $s/d$ and $s$ are continuous, with $|sy/d| \le B$, $0 \le s/d \le 1$ and $0 \le s \le 1$. Weak convergence of $F_r$ to $F$ therefore gives $A_r \to b\mu$, $B_r \to b$ and $n_r/N_r \to \Pr[S = 1] > 0$ (in probability when the $F_r$ are random). (e) [Ratio bound] If $b > 0$ and $B_r \ge b/2$, then $\left|\frac{A_r}{B_r} - \mu\right| = \frac{|A_r - \mu B_r|}{B_r} \le \frac{2}{b}\left(|A_r - b\mu| + |\mu|\,|B_r - b|\right)$. With $t = \epsilon b/[4(1 + |\mu|)]$ this gives $\Pr(|\hat\mu_{VH,r} - \mu| > \epsilon) \le \Pr(|B_r - b| \ge b/2) + \Pr(|A_r - b\mu| \ge t) + \Pr(|B_r - b| \ge t)$; the event $n_r = 0$ is contained in $\{|B_r - b| \ge b/2\}$, since then $B_r = 0$. (f) [Deterministic limit] If $A_r \to b\mu$ and $B_r \to b \ne 0$, then $A_r/B_r \to \mu$. (g) [Degree support of the limit] $bk = \Pr[S = 1|D = k] \le 1$ gives $k \le 1/b$ for every $k \in A$.
canonical_claim.note: The paper prints no proof beyond the sentence introducing the corollary. A formal statement needs the convergence premise and the bounds made explicit; the following is the audit's formal reading, which is the validators' and is not printed in the paper. Hypotheses: (H1) [common bounds] there are constants $B < \infty$ and $K < \infty$ with $|y_{rj}| \le B$ and $d_{rj} \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ for all $r$ and $j$; (H2) [the standing convergence of Section 2] the joint empirical laws $F_r$ converge weakly to a fixed law $F$ of $(Y, D, S)$, in probability if they are random; (H3) $F$ satisfies Condition 1; (H4) $F$ satisfies Condition 2 with $f(k) = ak$, $a \ne 0$, that is, $\Pr[S = 1|D = k] = bk$ for $k \in A$ with $b = ca$. Conclusion: $\hat\mu_{VH,r} \to \mathrm{E}_F[Y]$, in probability when the $F_r$ are random (the value assigned to $\hat\mu_{VH,r}$ when $n_r = 0$ does not matter). The deterministic case contains all of the mathematics; the in-probability case adds only the union bound of item (e). The exact content is items (a) to (g); the limit step uses only that the two bounded continuous functionals of item (d) converge. Why the hypotheses must be explicit. (i) Bounds (finding P021-E001; it is rated a clarity note, so there is no counterexample or corrected-statement target). The setting introduces bounded $Y$ and $D \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ with ‘Without loss of generality’ and, read literally, bounds only the limiting $Y$. The validator showed that these are restrictions and that a bound on the limit alone is not enough: for $m \ge 1$ take $N = 3m$ units, all of degree 1, sample $n = m$ of them, give one sampled unit the outcome $2m$ and every other unit the outcome $0$. The joint empirical laws converge weakly to mass $2/3$ at $(Y, D, S) = (0, 1, 0)$ and $1/3$ at $(0, 1, 1)$, a law with bounded $Y$ that satisfies Conditions 1 and 2 with $f(1) = 1$, $c = 1/3$ and has $\mathrm{E}[Y] = 0$; yet $A_m = 2/3$, $B_m = 1/3$ and $\hat\mu_{VH} = 2$ for every $m$ (recomputed exactly when this list was fixed). (H1) excludes this sequence, and the validator judged a bound common to the sequence to be the natural reading, under which the corollary is correct. (H1) is the validator's sufficient formulation; its degree bound is stronger than necessary, since with $|y_{rj}| \le B$ and positive integer degrees one has $|sy/d| \le B$ and $0 \le s/d \le 1$ whatever $K$ is, and item (g) bounds the degree support of the limit; a uniform-integrability condition on $sy/d$ can replace the common outcome bound. (ii) Convergence (candidate P021-N004, not confirmed by either validator). Conditions 1 and 2 are conditions on the limit $F$ of the realized empirical laws, not on design-averaged inclusion probabilities. In the two-component example behind that candidate the law averaged over a fair coin satisfies both conditions with $c = 1/8$, $f(k) = k$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y] = 9/20$, while $\hat\mu_{VH}$ tends to $7/10$ or to $1/5$ with probability $1/2$ each; the example violates (H2), and Condition 1 fails in each realized limit, so it is not a counterexample to the corollary. (iii) The indicator (candidate P021-N002, not confirmed). $S$ is a 0/1 indicator in the joint law and (H3) makes $\Pr[S = 1] > 0$ in the limit; how $S$ represents a with-replacement sample in which a subject can appear more than once (p. 100) is not specified in the paper, and nothing in this target depends on it. (iv) Index range. $f(k) = ak$ has no zero on $\{1, \ldots, K\}$, so the $0/0$ of finding P021-N003 does not arise; Condition 2 is still needed only on $A$. Evidence. Complete derivations: the artifact named here, section 4 (consistency under common bounds) and section 5 (the exact failure when only the limit is bounded; script check.py and output check-output.txt in the same folder), and runs/P021/validate/P021-N004/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 1–4. An auxiliary Lean file written by the second validator of P021-N004, runs/P021/validate/P021-N004/v2/artifact/check.lean, proves the finite-stratum algebra of items (a) and (b) and the ratio limit of item (f) for stratum-level sequences (its saved output, lean_output.txt, lists only the standard axioms). It does not state the empirical measures, the weak-convergence step of item (d) or Conditions 1 and 2 as conditions on a law, so it is a starting point and not a formalization of the corollary; the first validator's Lean attempt timed out and is not evidence. Both fresh readers report that the claim held up with a caveat: one on whether the convergence premise is listed (P021-N004), the other on the common bounds (P021-E001) and on the indicator (P021-N002).
